subject: Data analysis advice; distance-based density estimation with covariates and random effects

messages.author: 02d195331194f5bd
messages.subject: Data analysis advice; distance-based density estimation with covariates and random effects
parts:
Hello, I have some questions regarding the best analysis approach for my data.

Goal: 
Estimate lizard densities and the effect of habitat covariates on lizard densities

Data: 
223 line transects with distance measurements for each animal
covariates measured at either the transect (site-level) or at the forest-fragment level

Complications:
1) Transects are distributed among 12 forest fragments - ideally a random effect of fragment id could account for this, but as I understand it from searching this forum, that's not possible in unmarked at this point (and I don't have the programming & stats skills to program this all into WinBUGS)
2) Transect surveys are repeated in one (and only one) of the forest fragments in a different season.  

Analysis options:
1) regarding random effects
    a) Ignore random effects: treat transects as fully independent, even if they occur in the same forest fragment.
    b) Average all site-level covariates to the forest-fragment scale (transects & covariate measurements were placed randomly within each fragment)
    c) estimate density at each site without covariates & then use GLMM to model density estimates as a function of covariates
2) regarding semi-repeated surveys:
    a) Include season as covariate  (with a random effect for fragment, I think this would be the easy solution)
    b) exclude 2nd season from main analysis & run 2nd analysis with both seasons, but only the forest fragment that has surveys from both seasons

I'm not sure how to weight the pros/cons of these approaches, so I welcome any suggests you may have.

Thanks,
Phil

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Data analysis advice; distance-based density estimation with covariates and random effects
parts:
I agree that learning BUGS can only be a good thing. In the meantime you could just treat 'fragment' as a fixed effect. Your estimates should be similar to what you would get by treating 'fragment' as a random effect, but you will not be able to make inferences to fragments that were not surveyed.

Richard
